questions.q: For P(n): 2^n < 1 x 2 x 3 x ... x n, what is the smallest positive integer n for which P(n) is true?
questions.explanation: Test the first few natural numbers as in the Exemplar objective problem. For n=1,2,3 the inequality is false, while for n=4, 16 < 24 is true. Therefore the smallest such n is 4.

questions.q: A student proves P(5) is true and also proves that P(k) implies P(k+1) for every natural number k >= 5. What can be concluded?
options: A) P(n) is true for all natural numbers
B) P(n) is true for all n >= 5
C) P(n) is true only for n > 5
questions.answer: B) P(n) is true for all n >= 5
questions.explanation: Mathematical induction can begin at a fixed natural number other than 1. Since the base case P(5) is established and the implication works for every k >= 5, the chain proves P(6), P(7), and so on. Thus P(n) is true for every n >= 5.

questions.q: If 2*4^(2n+1) + 3^(3n+1) is divisible by the same positive integer lambda for all n in N, what is lambda according to the Exemplar calculation?
questions.explanation: Evaluate the expression for n=1 and n=2, obtaining 209 and 4235. Their HCF is 11, so 11 is the common divisor identified by the Exemplar. Hence lambda = 11.

questions.q: For P(n): 49^n + 16^n + k is divisible by 64 for all n in N, what is the least negative integral value of k?
questions.explanation: Use the first admissible value n=1. Then 49 + 16 + k = 65 + k must be divisible by 64. Choosing k = -1 gives 64, so the least negative integral value required is -1.
